segments.title: How the Royal Navy shaped the Skua specification
segments.summary: The Skua's 1934 order used a new operational requirement process that gave the Royal Navy direct control over aircraft specifications.
segments.body: The Skua was ordered in 1934 under the operational requirement process, which gave the Royal Navy direct control over aircraft specifications. Previously, the Navy had told the Air Ministry what it wanted and left the ministry to write the specification. That process involved lengthy exchanges and debate. The Navy had obtained aircraft capable of dive bombing, but it had been unable to secure a purpose-built dive bomber.

evidence.note: The Royal Navy gained direct control through operational requirements after an Air Ministry-led process had provided aircraft capable of dive bombing without a purpose-built dive bomber.

segments.title: Henderson's fighter-dive-bomber specification
segments.summary: Henderson drew on his experience as Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers to help shape the Skua's fighter-dive-bomber requirement.
segments.body: Rear Admiral Henderson had been Third Sea Lord since 1933. As a former Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers, he brought carrier experience to the new operational requirement process. He became closely involved in drafting the specification. The resulting requirement was for a fighter-dive-bomber, combining both roles in one aircraft.

evidence.note: Henderson had been Third Sea Lord since 1933 and used his experience as Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers to help write the fighter-dive-bomber specification.

segments.title: The Skua's Bristol Perseus engine and Browning armament
segments.summary: The Skua's engine and armament were probably its weaknesses. Improvements to both, with slightly greater speed and range, could have made it a very capable aircraft.
segments.body: The Skua had an 890-horsepower Bristol Perseus XII engine. Its armament appears to have comprised four .303-inch Browning machine guns. The engine and armament were probably its main weaknesses. Improving both, with slightly more speed and range, would probably have made the Skua a very capable aircraft.

evidence.note: The engine and guns are suggested as probable weaknesses, with higher speed and longer range part of a conditional improvement. The gun count, calibre and Browning name are reconstructed from garbled wording at 1:23-1:26 and need audiovisual confirmation.

segments.title: Königsberg and the Skua's short technological lead
segments.summary: The Skua sank Königsberg and achieved more than its reputation suggests, yet rapid change in aircraft design soon overtook a type that had begun at the leading edge.
segments.body: The Skua achieved a great deal, including the sinking of Königsberg. It was at the leading edge of aircraft design during a period of rapid technological change. It was quickly surpassed, yet remained a good aircraft.

evidence.note: The opening describes the Skua's poor reputation, which the closing assessment challenges.
The transcript cites the sinking of Königsberg and describes the Skua as a rapidly surpassed but still good aircraft.
